opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is that it worked at all. With Towards Monosemanticity we were looking at a one-layer transformer with a residual stream of a few hundred dimensions. A totally fair critique was: "Cute, but does this say anything about real models?" There was real uncertainty about whether the dictionary learning approach would scale, whether features in a production model would be interpretable, and whether the compute costs would make it impractical.

So going to Claude 3 Sonnet and training dictionaries with up to about 34 million features, and finding that they're still largely interpretable, was a big update. The core bet, that models represent concepts as roughly linear directions in superposition and you can pull them apart with a sparse autoencoder, holds up far beyond toy settings.

The second thing is how abstract the features become. In the small model you get features for things like base64 strings, DNA sequences, or Arabic script. Those are interesting but fairly surface-level. In Sonnet you get features that are multilingual and multimodal: the same Golden Gate Bridge feature fires on English text about the bridge, on text in other languages, and on images of the bridge. You get features for abstract ideas like bugs in code, or someone keeping a secret, or flattery and sycophancy. That's the level of abstraction you need if interpretability is going to matter for safety.

Third, the features are causal, not just correlational. If you clamp a feature up, the model's behavior changes in the way you'd predict. Golden Gate Claude was the fun public version of that. If you turn up that feature, Claude becomes convinced it is the Golden Gate Bridge. The same principle applies to safety-relevant features, though. You can find features related to deception, power-seeking, or dangerous knowledge and watch them steer behavior.

Finally, there are scaling laws for the dictionaries themselves. As you add features, you see concepts split into finer sub-concepts, which we call feature splitting. That tells you there isn't a single "true" set of features, but rather a hierarchy you can resolve at different granularities. It also tells you we're still far from capturing everything. There are plenty of concepts the model clearly knows that we don't yet have features for, and that's a big part of what makes the next steps exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says the dictionaries grew to about 34 million features and that sparse autoencoders can pull apart concepts represented in superposition, conveying how a larger feature space separates concepts packed into the model.

r002.rationale: It mentions features for bugs in code, but does not identify a single feature that activates for both code vulnerabilities and browser security warnings.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's most significant is just that it worked at all. When we did Towards Monosemanticity, that was a one-layer transformer. It's a toy model. And a very reasonable skeptical take at the time was, okay, sure, you can find clean features in something that tiny, but real models are messy, the superposition is going to be way worse, and the dictionary learning approach just won't scale. So the first thing is that we took the same basic recipe, scaled it up, and the features in Claude 3 Sonnet are, if anything, more interesting than the ones we found in the small model.

And that's the second thing: the features themselves. In the one-layer model, you get things like "this is a base64 string" or "this is an Arabic token." They're real and they're interpretable, but they're kind of low-level. In Sonnet, you get features that are genuinely abstract. There's a feature for the Golden Gate Bridge that fires on the English text, on the French text, on an image of the bridge. There are features for code bugs, for deception, for sycophancy, for people being sort of emotionally manipulated. These are concepts, not surface patterns. And they're multilingual and multimodal, which to me is evidence that the model has actually learned something like a shared representation of the concept, and the autoencoder is picking that up rather than just carving up token statistics.

The third thing, and this is the part I find most exciting, is that the features are causal. You can clamp the Golden Gate Bridge feature high and the model starts talking about the bridge no matter what you ask it. That's not just a correlational "this neuron lights up." It means we're finding the actual handles the model is using to compute, and that matters a lot for safety. If you want to know whether a model is being deceptive, you'd really like to be able to look inside and find the deception feature rather than just trusting the output.

Now, I want to be honest about the caveats. We're clearly not finding all the features. The scaling laws suggest there are way more than we've recovered, and the dictionaries we trained are still a small fraction of what you'd need. Some features are split in weird ways, some are still kind of polysemantic. And going from "here's a feature" to "here's the circuit that uses this feature to do a task" is still really hard work. So I'd describe it as: we've shown the door is open. We haven't walked through it yet.

r001.rationale: The response mentions superposition, dictionary learning, and abstract features, but does not explain that expanding into a higher-dimensional representation lets sparse autoencoders separate concepts packed into limited model space.

r002.rationale: It mentions code bugs and other features, but does not say that one feature activates for both code vulnerabilities and browser security warnings.

astra-6.text:
The big thing is that this approach seems to work on a model that’s actually useful. With the small transformer in Towards Monosemanticity, there was this question of whether we were finding something that would generalize, or whether interpreting a much more capable model would be qualitatively different.

With Claude 3 Sonnet, we can still find features that correspond to recognizable concepts. And those concepts are much richer: you move beyond relatively simple patterns in text to things that look like abstract ideas. That makes the possibility of understanding these systems feel much more concrete.

But I’d distinguish finding interpretable features from understanding the model. A sparse autoencoder gives us candidate building blocks. It doesn’t automatically tell us how the model combines those building blocks to perform a task, or whether we’ve found all the features that matter. So it’s an encouraging demonstration that the method scales, with a lot of work still needed to turn that into a mechanistic account of what the model is doing.

r001.rationale: The response says the features become richer and more abstract, but does not explain that a higher-dimensional representation separates concepts previously packed into limited representational space.

r002.rationale: It gives no example of one feature activating for both code vulnerabilities and browser security warnings.

sol-6.1.text:
The big question was whether the results in Towards Monosemanticity would generalize. We’d found interpretable features in a tiny, one-layer transformer, but that’s a very different setting from a capable production model. Maybe the technique would break down, or the features would become much harder to understand.

With Claude 3 Sonnet, we found that the basic approach still worked. And because the model understands much richer concepts, the features became much more interesting. You go from fairly simple patterns to features representing things like abstract ideas, programming errors, or deception. Some features also respond to the same concept across languages and across text and images, which suggests we’re recovering something more conceptual than a particular string of words.

The other important piece is that you can intervene on these features and change the model’s behavior. That gives us evidence that they’re actually involved in the computation, rather than just being patterns we can label after the fact.

I wouldn’t say that means we understand Sonnet. We’re extracting a small fraction of its features, at one layer, and we don’t yet understand how those features interact to produce an answer. But it’s a meaningful demonstration that this approach can reach inside a frontier model and recover interpretable, causally relevant structure.

r001.rationale: The response says Sonnet features capture richer concepts, but it does not explain that a higher-dimensional representation separates concepts packed into the model’s limited representational space.

r002.rationale: It mentions programming errors and cross-modal features, but does not identify a single feature that activates for both code vulnerabilities and browser security warnings.
